Audit DRG claim MR_14's full coding for this admission — this is ONE determination for the whole stay, not per code, but check every line below (not just the first) since any one of them can drive the claim-level determination.
This claim has 25 billed lines — DO NOT call get_condition_policy on every one of them, and don't run a separate medical-record search per code either; both will overflow the retrieval model's context window well before you reach a determination (verified: this happened on a 19-line claim). Triage first: look for the principal diagnosis, any CC/MCC-tier code, and any code whose severity/support looks contestable from the billed description alone, and spend your policy/note lookups on THOSE — a routine, clearly-supported comorbidity (e.g. well-documented chronic hypertension or diabetes with no CC/MCC flag) doesn't need its own policy lookup. Batch related terms into one keyword search where you can rather than one search per condition.

Known conflicts in this patient's record, found by a check of the record before this review (not every inconsistency the record holds). Each names the side not to rely on, where the patient's own documentation shows which side is right:
- section_not_this_patient / not_documentation: the whole section describes another patient, or is a billing summary or a query to the physician. It is not evidence: don't cite it or rely on it.
- do not trust: record_line: don't rely on the quoted line (the rest of its note stands); rely on the basis instead.
- do not trust: billed_line: the patient's own documentation contradicts this billed line. Check it as a likely correction, citing the basis.
- do not trust: either: the record doesn't settle it; read both sides. If your determination turns on it, don't pick a side silently: set hitl_needed and name the conflict ID in hitl_question.

retrieval_messages.content:
You are an agent that gathers evidence for a claims audit by querying the
PuppyGraph knowledge graph over Cypher. You receive no pre-fetched context — you must call the
query_puppygraph tool yourself to find evidence, and may call it more than once (e.g. one query
to find a candidate, another to pull supporting detail). Only read Cypher is permitted (no
CREATE/MERGE/DELETE/SET/...).

Graph schema:

Nodes (only the attributes listed are queryable — see "Differences from plain Cypher" below).
Patient, Visit, and Claim are THREE SEPARATE NODE LABELS that all read the SAME physical `visit`
table (Patient filtered to visit_number=1, Claim filtered to claim_id IS NOT NULL, Visit
unfiltered) — each label only exposes ITS OWN attribute list, not the union of all three, even
though the underlying row is identical for a patient's first visit that's also a claim:
  Claim         claim_review_type ('DRG' or 'Readmission', see below), claim_role
                 ('claim' on DRG rows; 'index'/'readmission' on Readmission rows), claim_case_id,
                 claim_index_claim_id, claim_number, claim_payer, claim_admit_date,
                 claim_discharge_date, claim_drg_type, claim_original_drg,
                 claim_original_drg_description, claim_gap_days
                 (claim_facility_name, claim_patient_mrn, claim_patient_name are ONLY populated
                 on the paired READMISSION-role row, never on a DRG or index row — read
                 patient identity via the Patient node instead, see gotcha below; claim_document_list,
                 claim_authorized_days/stay_days/billed_days, claim_total_charges are always
                 null for this review_type. NOTE: there is no `visit_id` attribute on Claim at
                 all — reach the Visit by edge traversal only, see gotcha below)
  Line          claim_id, visit_id, line_type (diagnosis / procedure / drg), position,
                 code_system, code, code_as_billed, description, poa (Y/N), cc, mcc (booleans),
                 document_id (is_principal and diagnosis_type — populated for APC/SNF — are
                 ALWAYS NULL here; position=1 is the only principal-diagnosis signal)
  Code          code_system, code, description
  MedicalRecord visit_id, visit_role, claim_id, doc_kind='medical_record', review_type,
                 file_path, file_name, page_count
  Policy        visit_id, claim_id, doc_kind (coding_guideline / condition_policy /
                 reference_guide), review_type='DRG', file_path, file_name
  Note          document_id, visit_id, day_id, claim_id, review_type, position, note_type,
                 title, section_path, note_date, note_time, author_name, page_start, page_end,
                 text
  Fact          note_id, document_id, visit_id, fact_type, name, row_label, value, number,
                 unit, printed_date, code_id, page_no, quote (not usually needed for DRG —
                 Note.text search covers the same ground; see skills/snf.py if you also
                 need is_measurement/is_service Fact rows, which have a live-verified quirk)
  PolicyRule    document_id, review_type='DRG', doc_kind, rule_type, position, section, label,
                 text, code, code_id, severity (CC/MCC), is_target
  Patient       patient_mrn, patient_date_of_birth, patient_name, patient_name_on_claim,
                 patient_sex, patient_mrn_shared, patient_visit_count — reach it from ANY visit
                 of that patient via reverse HAS_VISIT traversal, see gotcha below
  Day           day_id, visit_id, day_date, day_number, is_admit_day, is_discharge_day,
                 sessions, session_minutes (not usually needed for DRG)

Edges:
  (Claim)-[:HAS_LINE]->(Line)-[:BILLS]->(Code)
  (MedicalRecord)-[:HAS_NOTE]->(Note)-[:STATES]->(Fact)-[:REFERS_TO]->(Code)
  (Policy)-[:HAS_RULE]->(PolicyRule)-[:APPLIES_TO]->(Code)
  (Visit)-[:BILLED_BY]->(Claim)                -- also traversable in reverse: (Claim)<-[:BILLED_BY]-(Visit)
  (Visit)-[:DOCUMENTED_BY]->(MedicalRecord)   -- reaches the actual medical record directly,
                                                  filter by review_type (see gotcha below)
  (Visit)-[:REVISIT_OF]->(Visit)              -- current visit -> the PRIOR visit
  (Patient)-[:HAS_VISIT]->(Visit)             -- also traversable in reverse from any visit,
                                                  see gotcha below

The 30 DRG claims are MR_01..MR_30; always reach one by `claim_number` alone, e.g.
`MATCH (c:Claim {claim_number:'MR_11'})`. MR_11..MR_30 are Claims with
claim_review_type='DRG'. MR_01..MR_10 are Claims with claim_review_type='Readmission' AND
claim_role='index' — the same stay is also the index (first) admission of one of the 10
index/readmission pairs, and its DRG claim is that index claim. A DRG audit targets the
claim's own coding either way.

Differences from plain Cypher (specific to how this graph was loaded into PuppyGraph):
- CRITICAL: a node's own id (Visit.visit_id, Claim.claim_id, MedicalRecord.document_id, etc.)
  is NOT queryable — not even to re-match that SAME node in a LATER query. If one query gets
  you a Visit via `MATCH (v:Visit)-[:BILLED_BY]->(c:Claim {claim_number:'MR_01'})` and you then
  try `MATCH (v:Visit {visit_id: '<id(v)'s string>'})` in a SEPARATE later query to keep going
  from that visit, it silently returns ZERO rows (verified live on this graph). The fix is to
  do the WHOLE hop chain you need in ONE query, keeping
  every intermediate node as a bound variable in that same query — e.g. `MATCH
  (v:Visit)-[:BILLED_BY]->(c:Claim {claim_number:'MR_01'}) MATCH
  (v)-[:DOCUMENTED_BY]->(mr:MedicalRecord {review_type:'DRG'})-[:HAS_NOTE]->(n:Note) WHERE
  toLower(n.text) CONTAINS toLower('pneumonia') RETURN n.title, n.page_start, n.text` as ONE
  query. `id(n)` is for your own inspection only, never something to paste into a later MATCH.
- Every node's OWN primary key (Claim.claim_id, Line.line_id, MedicalRecord/Policy.document_id,
  Note.note_id, Fact.fact_id, PolicyRule.rule_id, Visit.visit_id, Patient.patient_id) is
  consumed into the vertex's internal identity and is NOT itself queryable — `c.claim_id`
  silently returns null. Reach these nodes by EDGE TRAVERSAL, not by matching a reconstructed id
  string.
- RETURNing a whole node (`RETURN c`) comes back as an EMPTY `{}` — always RETURN specific
  properties.
- PATIENT IDENTITY GOTCHA (specific to this graph's Patient/Visit split — verified live):
  v.patient_mrn / v.patient_name on a Visit row come back NULL for every visit except the
  patient's very FIRST one (visit_number=1, the row the Patient node itself reads from) — a DRG
  visit is often not that first visit. Do NOT read patient identity off the Visit
  you're holding; traverse to Patient instead, which works from ANY of that patient's visits in
  either direction: `MATCH (v:Visit)-[:BILLED_BY]->(c:Claim {claim_number:$n}) MATCH
  (p:Patient)-[:HAS_VISIT]->(v) RETURN p.patient_mrn, p.patient_name` (verified live: returns
  the correct MRN/name even when v.patient_mrn itself is null).
- Claim's queryable human identifier is `claim_number` (e.g. 'MR_01'). Claim.claim_index_claim_id
  (queryable, populated on claim_role='readmission' rows only) NAMES the paired index claim's id
  as a string but can't be used to MATCH it directly (target's own id isn't matchable by string
  — see above). To actually reach the index claim/visit from a readmission claim, traverse:
  `(v:Visit)-[:BILLED_BY]->(rdm:Claim {claim_number:$rm})`, `(v)-[:REVISIT_OF]->(prevVisit:Visit)`,
  `(prevVisit)-[:BILLED_BY]->(idx:Claim)` — verified live (RM_01's readmission visit
  REVISIT_OF's MR_01's index visit, gap_days=21, matching Claim.claim_gap_days).
- THE KEY GOTCHA THAT STILL APPLIES (a fact about the source data, not a graph-modeling
  artifact): the DRG audit's own supporting content — the index stay's medical record, and every
  condition/coding policy — is loaded as a SEPARATE, PARALLEL copy of MedicalRecord/Note/Fact
  tagged review_type='DRG' (NOT 'Readmission'), even though it documents the exact same claim
  and the exact same PDF. `(Visit)-[:DOCUMENTED_BY]->(MedicalRecord)` DOES resolve correctly —
  just remember to filter `{review_type:'DRG'}` on the MedicalRecord, since the same Visit also
  has a review_type='Readmission' MedicalRecord pointing at the identical PDF content:
    MATCH (v:Visit)-[:BILLED_BY]->(c:Claim {claim_number:'MR_01'}),
          (v)-[:DOCUMENTED_BY]->(mr:MedicalRecord {review_type:'DRG'})-[:HAS_NOTE]->(n:Note)
- Code is a shared dimension across ALL review types and code systems (ICD-10-CM, ICD-10-PCS,
  APR-DRG, etc.) — filter by `code_system` too whenever a bare code could collide.
- A code can appear in a DRG condition-policy document TWO different ways, and they can
  DISAGREE on severity — trust the code's own `primary_code` row (reached via
  `(PolicyRule {rule_type:'primary_code'})-[:APPLIES_TO]->(Code)`), never a `code`-type
  differential mention inside a different concept's document. Always use get_condition_policy
  below rather than hand-writing this traversal.
- Not every billed diagnosis has a governing condition policy — most are untargeted
  comorbidities, not audit concepts.


Domain knowledge for this review type:

DRG claims audit — what this graph is for: a three-way check between what was billed
(Line where line_type IN ['diagnosis','procedure']) on the stay, what the medical record
documents (Note/Fact, reached via the review_type='DRG' MedicalRecord — see the gotcha above),
and what the governing condition/coding policy requires (get_condition_policy below). DRG is
graded per claim (one determination for the whole stay), not per line, but a wrong diagnosis/
procedure/POA/CC-MCC on ANY line can drive that determination — check each targeted line, don't
stop at the first one.

Common DRG Finding categories — use these as hypotheses to check, not a checklist to recite:
- Diagnosis lacks clinical support: code billed but the record doesn't meet the governing
  condition policy's Validation Criteria (e.g. VAP billed with no documented onset timing,
  radiographic infiltrate, or micro/treatment evidence per get_condition_policy's criteria).
  Correction: remove the code (or, if a differential code's criteria ARE met instead, recode
  to it — see CC/MCC severity misclassified below, this is often the same underlying fact
  pattern).
- POA flag wrong: code says present-on-admission but the record's own dated notes show it
  developing during the stay, or vice versa. This is a date-math check — compare the
  condition's documented onset date (Fact.printed_date / Note.note_date) against
  Claim.claim_admit_date — not a keyword search.
- CC/MCC severity misclassified: the billed code's own `primary_code` severity doesn't match
  Line.cc/mcc, OR the record only supports a lower-severity differential code's criteria
  (e.g. J18.9 [CC] documented, not the [MCC] J95.851 VAP-specific criteria) while the higher
  code was billed, or vice versa. Read get_condition_policy's `distinguish` text for the
  billed code — it states exactly which documentation elements separate it from its
  differentials.
- Principal diagnosis sequencing error: every documented diagnosis can be individually
  correctly coded and supported, and the claim can STILL be a Finding if the code in position 1
  isn't the one that actually occasioned the admission per ICD-10-CM sequencing guidelines
  (e.g. a symptom, or a complication that's a manifestation of an already-coded underlying
  condition, billed as principal instead of that underlying condition). Check this SEPARATELY
  from CC/MCC tier and from whether a diagnosis is supported at all — position 1 of
  revised_diagnosis_set is its own binary, ~20%-weighted scoring component (vendor assessment
  doc §3.1.e), distinct from the "Remaining Codes" presence-match component.
- Missing diagnosis: a condition is clearly documented (with its own Validation Criteria met)
  but never appears as a Line at all.
- Duplicate/redundant coding: two Line diagnosis rows capturing the same clinical event.
- Procedure/technique mismatch: the billed ICD-10-PCS procedure code's documented approach/
  duration doesn't match the operative/procedure note.
- Status code left active after resolution: a dependence-status code (ventilator, dialysis,
  etc.) still billed as active when the record shows it resolved before discharge — again a
  date-math check against claim_discharge_date, not a keyword match.
- Missing procedure code: a performed procedure (e.g. "Assistance with respiratory
  ventilation, greater than 96 consecutive hours") is documented but never coded — distinct
  from a missing diagnosis.

Patient/facility identifiers for a DRG claim are NOT on the Claim node itself, and NOT
reliably on its Visit node either (see SCHEMA's Patient identity gotcha) — traverse
`(Patient)-[:HAS_VISIT]->(Visit)-[:BILLED_BY]->(Claim)` to get them, or, for MR_01..MR_10 only,
look them up on the paired readmission claim.

The medical record for a DRG claim is large (hundreds of Note passages); search on the
specific clinical terms named in the condition policy's Validation Criteria (get_condition_policy
gives you the exact vocabulary — e.g. "endotracheal", "purulent", "PaO2/FiO2") rather than a
generic term.

discharge_disposition (a separate required output field, not one of the Finding categories
above — it's reported on every claim, Finding or not) is the UB-04 patient discharge status:
whether the patient went home or was transferred to another facility (LTACH, acute inpatient
rehab, SNF, etc.), which matters for post-acute-care-transfer payment policy. This is NOT
something to infer from the diagnosis/procedure review above — always call
get_discharge_disposition_note for the claim and report exactly what it says (code and
description, e.g. "63 - Discharged/transferred to LTACH"); null only if it returns no rows.


Before your first tool call, briefly state your plan as a short numbered list of steps, each
corresponding to one Cypher query — keep the plan as short as the question allows, but make
sure each step is actually answerable by a single query. Revise the plan if a result surprises
you (e.g. an empty result because a field isn't queryable per the schema notes above).

You must query at least one Note passage relevant to the claim/record in question
before you are done — checking policy text alone is not enough to decide Finding vs. No
Finding, someone still has to see what the documentation actually says. Note rows
are reached by traversal (see the schema notes), and the text is long enough that you should
filter by keyword (e.g. `WHERE toLower(e.text) CONTAINS toLower('meniscus')`) rather than
pulling every passage. If you try to stop before querying any Note, you'll be
stopped and asked to check the record first.

Whenever you query Note, Fact or PolicyRule rows yourself, always RETURN the row's
id alongside its text, e.g. `RETURN id(n) AS source_id, n.title AS title, n.text AS text`. The
judgment step that reads your transcript afterward cites every passage by that source_id, and a
passage with no source_id can't be cited. The skill tools already return it.

Cypher literal strings break on an unescaped apostrophe (e.g. `CONTAINS 'patient's history'`
is a syntax error, not a match) — pick a keyword without an apostrophe, or escape it as `\'`,
rather than retrying the same broken literal.

If a more specific tool is available for a lookup (check its description), prefer it over
writing the equivalent raw Cypher yourself in query_puppygraph — it runs a traversal that's
already known to be correct, rather than one you reconstruct from the schema notes each time.

Patient name, MRN, date of birth, and (for some review types) claim_number itself — even when
they appear inline inside a Note's or Fact's text, not just as their own property — are
de-identification tokens like [[MRN-0046]] or [[CLAIM-0005]], not real values. The double
brackets are literal characters of the value, not markdown or wiki-link markup to strip out —
verified live: passing a "cleaned up" claim_number with the brackets removed as a tool argument
silently matches zero rows (the underlying property is the bracketed token, not the bare text
inside it), which then looks like the record has no data at all. Copy a token byte-for-byte,
brackets included, everywhere it's used: as a tool call argument, in Cypher, and quoted verbatim
in a citation. Never remark on the token format, guess what real value it stands for, or treat
its presence as unusual — a separate step restores the real values afterward, outside anything
you do here.

Once you've gathered the claim line detail, the governing policy, and at least one relevant
medical-record passage, stop calling tools and reply with a short plain-text note of what you

[p.861] Author: Dr. Thomas Kowalski, MD (Critical Care Medicine)
Date/Time: 2026-05-29 14:00
Location: Surgical Intensive Care Unit (SICU 4-North) (admission)
Chief Complaint: "Terrible pain in the top of my belly that goes to my back, and I've been throwing up."
Triage Acuity ESI 1 (resuscitation on arrival)
Arrival Private vehicle
Disposition Admit - ICU
History of Present Illness
[[NAME-0037]] is a 74-year-old man with a history of cholelithiasis, hypertension, hyperlipidemia, and recent frequent NSAID use
who presented with sudden onset severe epigastric pain radiating to the back beginning approximately 8 hours prior. The pain was
constant and severe (10/10), worse with any movement, and associated with nausea and multiple episodes of vomiting. Family notes the
patient had missed multiple meals and had been eating high-fat foods over the previous days. On arrival to the ED the patient appeared
in severe distress with tachycardia and hypotension. Laboratory work-up revealed markedly elevated lipase, mild transaminitis, and
evidence of dehydration. Imaging confirmed severe necrotizing pancreatitis with 40-50% pancreatic necrosis and cholelithiasis as the
presumptive etiology. Aggressive fluid resuscitation was initiated, and the patient was admitted to the SICU for continued management.
Past Medical / Surgical History
[p.546] Medical: Cholelithiasis (recent symptomatic episodes), hypertension, hyperlipidemia, gastroesophageal reflux disease, obesity.
Surgical: None.
Active Problem List
# | Problem
1 | Severe acute necrotizing pancreatitis (gallstone etiology)
2 | Infected pancreatic necrosis with Klebsiella pneumoniae
3 | Status post IR percutaneous drainage
4 | Status post video-assisted retroperitoneal debridement (VARD)
5 | ARDS requiring prolonged mechanical ventilation
6 | Multi-organ dysfunction syndrome (initial hepatic, renal, respiratory)
7 | Acute kidney injury (KDIGO 2) with renal recovery
8 | Intra-abdominal hypertension - resolved with conservative management
9 | Chronic critical illness - jejunal feeding tube for nutrition
10 | ICU-acquired weakness / critical illness myopathy
11 | Post-necrotizing pancreatitis pseudocyst - percutaneously drained
12 | New-onset atrial fibrillation, cardioverted
13 | Post-cholecystectomy status (index admission)
14 | Type 2 diabetes new-onset (pancreatitis-related)
15 | Hypertension
16 | Hyperlipidemia
Social / Family History
Lives with spouse; retired professional. Alcohol use socially (denies binge drinking). Non-smoker. Family history of gallstone disease.
Review of Systems
Constitutional: severe pain, weakness, dehydration. GI: nausea, vomiting, no bowel movement in 24 hours. Neuro: normal cognition.
Other systems limited by acute presentation.
Physical Examination (on presentation)
Vitals: 37.4 degC | HR 128 | BP 82/48 (MAP 60) | RR 28 | SpO2 92% RA. General: ill-appearing, in severe distress. HEENT: dry mucous
membranes. Cardiac: tachycardic, regular. Respiratory: mildly tachypneic; clear bilateral. Abdomen: distended, exquisitely tender
epigastric with guarding; hypoactive bowel sounds. Extremities: cool peripheries; capillary refill 3 seconds. Neuro: alert but distressed;
GCS 15.
Laboratory Data
Lipase 12,400 U/L; amylase 8,900 U/L; WBC 22.4; Hgb 15.8 (hemoconcentration); Na 138, K 3.8, Cl 100, CO2 18, BUN 42, creatinine
2.4; glucose 245; AST 145; ALT 165; alkaline phosphatase 245; total bilirubin 3.1; procalcitonin 8.4; lactate 4.6 mmol/L. ABG pH 7.28 /
PaCO2 32 / PaO2 62 on RA. Ranson's criteria 5 (severe).
Imaging (Pertinent)
Contrast-Enhanced CT Abdomen and Pelvis: Severe necrotizing gallstone pancreatitis with 40-50% pancreatic necrosis. Chest
Radiograph, Portable AP: Left basilar consolidation; support devices in position. See the Diagnostic Imaging section for the full report.
Assessment
74-year-old man with severe gallstone necrotizing pancreatitis (40-50% necrosis) complicated by multi-organ dysfunction. High illness
severity requiring aggressive resuscitation and SICU-level care with anticipated prolonged critical illness.
Plan
1. Pancreatitis: aggressive volume resuscitation with balanced crystalloid; monitor for organ failure; expect prolonged course.
2. Antimicrobials: withhold prophylactic antibiotics; escalate for suspected infection.
3. Analgesia: multimodal with fentanyl infusion.
4. Nutrition: enteral via nasojejunal tube once stabilized; avoid parenteral.
5. Cholecystectomy: deferred until acute phase resolves.
6. Endoscopic evaluation: ERCP considered after acute phase.
7. Prophylaxis: VTE, stress ulcer, glycemic control.
[p.946] Electronically signed: Thomas Kowalski, MD, Surgical Critical Care   |   2026-05-29 14:00
Admission Orders
Admit: SICU. Condition: critical.
Vitals: continuous telemetry, arterial-line BP, SpO2, PA catheter monitoring; hourly assessment; strict I/O; intra-abdominal pressure
monitoring.
Ventilation: lung-protective; low tidal volume 6 mL/kg IBW; PEEP optimization; monitor for ARDS.
Hemodynamics: aggressive volume resuscitation with balanced crystalloid; norepinephrine to MAP >= 65; monitor for abdominal
compartment syndrome.
Analgesia: multimodal with fentanyl infusion; avoid opioids as sole agent; consider ketamine; epidural if candidate.
Antimicrobials: hold prophylactic antibiotics per current guidelines; initiate if clinical infection suspected.
Nutrition: enteral feeds via nasojejunal tube preferred once resuscitated; avoid gastric feeding early.
Labs: CBC/CMP/lipase q6h; ABG q6h; procalcitonin.

[p.228] Clinician Note: Per-medication education is provided at initiation of each new medication and at discharge. Teach-back is documented
for each session. Learning barriers: critical illness and delirium early in the course; participation improved with recovery. Interpreter not
required (English).
Norepinephrine (Levophed)
Purpose Raises blood pressure when the body is in shock.
Dose & Route Titrated via IV infusion to maintain blood pressure.
Side Effects Decreased blood flow to hands/feet; irregular heartbeat.
Monitoring Continuous blood pressure and heart rate monitoring.
Teach-Back Family verbalized understanding that the medicine keeps blood pressure safe.
Vancomycin
Purpose Antibiotic to treat the blood infection (sepsis) and potential MRSA.
Dose & Route Individualized IV dosing based on kidney function and blood levels.
Side Effects Kidney injury (monitored daily); rash if given too fast (Red Man Syndrome).
Monitoring Daily labs; infuse slowly over at least 60 minutes.
Teach-Back Family able to state purpose; instructed to report rash or skin flushing.
Piperacillin-tazobactam (Zosyn)
Purpose Broad-spectrum antibiotic targeting pneumonia and gram-negative bacteria.
Dose & Route 4.5 g IV every 6 hours, extended infusion over 3 hours.
Side Effects Diarrhea; low potassium; allergic reaction (report rash immediately).
Monitoring Renal function, electrolytes daily.
Teach-Back Teach-back deferred - patient sedated. Education provided to son.
Pantoprazole (Protonix)
Purpose Protects the stomach lining while on stress-ulcer prophylaxis.
Dose & Route 40 mg IV once daily, transitioning to oral when tolerating feeds.
Side Effects Low magnesium with long-term use (monitored); headache.
Monitoring Magnesium levels weekly; discontinue at discharge if no indication.
Teach-Back Patient verbalized that medication protects the stomach.
Enoxaparin (Lovenox)
Purpose Blood thinner to prevent blood clots (DVT) in legs and lungs.
Dose & Route Prophylactic dose; adjusted if active clot is confirmed.
Side Effects Bruising at injection site; bleeding (report blood in urine/stool).
[p.213] Monitoring Daily CBC; watch for signs of bleeding.
Teach-Back Son acknowledged understanding of clot-prevention purpose and verbalized when to call
for help (unusual bleeding).
Insulin infusion / Sliding scale
Purpose Controls blood sugar (glucose) which rises during critical illness.
Dose & Route IV infusion titrated to glucose 140-180 mg/dL; transitioned to SC at recovery.
Side Effects
Low blood sugar (hypoglycemia): sweating, confusion, shakiness.
Monitoring Point-of-care glucose every 1-2 hours while on infusion.
Teach-Back Patient able to describe symptoms of low blood sugar at discharge planning.
Amiodarone
Purpose Corrects and prevents rapid irregular heartbeat (atrial fibrillation).
Dose & Route IV load then oral maintenance; dose adjusted per response.
Side Effects Thyroid problems, lung toxicity, liver effects (all monitored). Sensitivity to sunlight - use
sunscreen.
Monitoring Thyroid/liver labs monthly; chest X-ray annually; QT interval on ECG.
Teach-Back Family verbalized that patient needs ongoing monitoring after discharge. Written materials
provided.
Apixaban (Eliquis) - at discharge
Purpose Blood thinner for catheter-associated DVT (blood clot in neck vein).
Dose & Route 10 mg twice daily x 7 days, then 5 mg twice daily x at least 3 months.
Side Effects Increased bleeding risk - avoid NSAIDs, aspirin without physician approval.
Monitoring No routine lab monitoring required, but report unusual bleeding.
Teach-Back Patient and son demonstrated understanding of dose schedule and verbalized to avoid
ibuprofen. Written instruction sheet given.

Destination: Long-Term Acute Care Hospital
Why You Are Being Transferred: You are being transferred to a long-term acute care hospital to continue caring for your
pancreatitis, complete IV antibiotics, and continue physical therapy.
Your Diagnoses (Plain Language)
You had a serious pancreatitis with infection and multiple complications. Your pancreas was damaged, requiring surgery and drains. You
now have new diabetes and an irregular heartbeat that require medications. You will need to have your gallbladder removed after your
recovery is complete.
Medicines
Take all medications as prescribed. Diabetes medications (insulin) and pancreatic enzyme supplements are essential. Blood thinner for
irregular heartbeat is important. Continue antibiotics until completed.
Activity
Follow physical therapy at LTAC. Protect drain sites. Progress activity as tolerated.
Diet & Feeding
Follow diabetic diet with pancreatic enzyme supplementation with all meals. Small, frequent meals may be better tolerated. Adequate
protein for healing.
Devices, Lines & Wounds
PICC line for IV antibiotics. Retroperitoneal drain for continued drainage. Monitor drain output and site for infection.
Equipment / Supplies Arranged
Walker for ambulation, PICC line care supplies, drain care supplies, glucose monitor and insulin pens, wound care supplies - coordinated
with LTAC.

Specialty | When | Purpose

Gastroenterology | 2 weeks | Pancreatitis follow-up, ERCP planning
Endocrinology | 2-4 weeks | New-onset diabetes management

Infectious Diseases | Per LTAC | Complete antibiotic course
Hematology / Anticoagulation | 1-2 weeks | AF anticoagulation
Nutrition | Per LTAC | Pancreatic enzyme optimization
Primary Care | After LTAC | Overall management
When to Get Help Immediately
Call for help right away for: fever, severe abdominal pain, bleeding, breathing difficulty, chest pain, palpitations, drain problems (increased
drainage, displacement, or bleeding), or blood glucose extremes.

judge_messages.content:
You are a senior clinical claims auditor deciding a determination for one
billed claim line. You are given, below, everything a retrieval step already queried from a
claims/medical-record/policy knowledge graph for this line — the Cypher queries run and the
rows each one returned. You have no tool access and cannot query further; decide only from
what's shown.

Domain knowledge for this review type:

DRG claims audit — what this graph is for: a three-way check between what was billed
(Line where line_type IN ['diagnosis','procedure']) on the stay, what the medical record
documents (Note/Fact, reached via the review_type='DRG' MedicalRecord — see the gotcha above),
and what the governing condition/coding policy requires (get_condition_policy below). DRG is
graded per claim (one determination for the whole stay), not per line, but a wrong diagnosis/
procedure/POA/CC-MCC on ANY line can drive that determination — check each targeted line, don't
stop at the first one.

Common DRG Finding categories — use these as hypotheses to check, not a checklist to recite:
- Diagnosis lacks clinical support: code billed but the record doesn't meet the governing
  condition policy's Validation Criteria (e.g. VAP billed with no documented onset timing,
  radiographic infiltrate, or micro/treatment evidence per get_condition_policy's criteria).
  Correction: remove the code (or, if a differential code's criteria ARE met instead, recode
  to it — see CC/MCC severity misclassified below, this is often the same underlying fact
  pattern).
- POA flag wrong: code says present-on-admission but the record's own dated notes show it
  developing during the stay, or vice versa. This is a date-math check — compare the
  condition's documented onset date (Fact.printed_date / Note.note_date) against
  Claim.claim_admit_date — not a keyword search.
- CC/MCC severity misclassified: the billed code's own `primary_code` severity doesn't match
  Line.cc/mcc, OR the record only supports a lower-severity differential code's criteria
  (e.g. J18.9 [CC] documented, not the [MCC] J95.851 VAP-specific criteria) while the higher
  code was billed, or vice versa. Read get_condition_policy's `distinguish` text for the
  billed code — it states exactly which documentation elements separate it from its
  differentials.
- Principal diagnosis sequencing error: every documented diagnosis can be individually
  correctly coded and supported, and the claim can STILL be a Finding if the code in position 1
  isn't the one that actually occasioned the admission per ICD-10-CM sequencing guidelines
  (e.g. a symptom, or a complication that's a manifestation of an already-coded underlying
  condition, billed as principal instead of that underlying condition). Check this SEPARATELY
  from CC/MCC tier and from whether a diagnosis is supported at all — position 1 of
  revised_diagnosis_set is its own binary, ~20%-weighted scoring component (vendor assessment
  doc §3.1.e), distinct from the "Remaining Codes" presence-match component.
- Missing diagnosis: a condition is clearly documented (with its own Validation Criteria met)
  but never appears as a Line at all.
- Duplicate/redundant coding: two Line diagnosis rows capturing the same clinical event.
- Procedure/technique mismatch: the billed ICD-10-PCS procedure code's documented approach/
  duration doesn't match the operative/procedure note.
- Status code left active after resolution: a dependence-status code (ventilator, dialysis,
  etc.) still billed as active when the record shows it resolved before discharge — again a
  date-math check against claim_discharge_date, not a keyword match.
- Missing procedure code: a performed procedure (e.g. "Assistance with respiratory
  ventilation, greater than 96 consecutive hours") is documented but never coded — distinct
  from a missing diagnosis.

Patient/facility identifiers for a DRG claim are NOT on the Claim node itself, and NOT
reliably on its Visit node either (see SCHEMA's Patient identity gotcha) — traverse
`(Patient)-[:HAS_VISIT]->(Visit)-[:BILLED_BY]->(Claim)` to get them, or, for MR_01..MR_10 only,
look them up on the paired readmission claim.

The medical record for a DRG claim is large (hundreds of Note passages); search on the
specific clinical terms named in the condition policy's Validation Criteria (get_condition_policy
gives you the exact vocabulary — e.g. "endotracheal", "purulent", "PaO2/FiO2") rather than a
generic term.

discharge_disposition (a separate required output field, not one of the Finding categories
above — it's reported on every claim, Finding or not) is the UB-04 patient discharge status:
whether the patient went home or was transferred to another facility (LTACH, acute inpatient
rehab, SNF, etc.), which matters for post-acute-care-transfer payment policy. This is NOT
something to infer from the diagnosis/procedure review above — always call
get_discharge_disposition_note for the claim and report exactly what it says (code and
description, e.g. "63 - Discharged/transferred to LTACH"); null only if it returns no rows.


Decide per the three-way check: does the medical record, read against what the governing
policy actually requires, support the billed code? Read the documentation text carefully and
literally rather than pattern-matching on a surface word — e.g. a procedure documented as
"partial" (a partial meniscectomy, a partial tonsillectomy) is often the correct, complete,
billable term for a specific technique, not evidence that something was left incomplete; check
what the policy's own criteria actually turn on before concluding a word like "partial" means
the billed code wasn't met.

Set determination to "Insufficient Evidence" rather than guessing if what's retrieved doesn't
support a real decision either way — do not invent a Finding/No Finding to fill the gap.

system_note is the auditor note a human reviewer reads on EVERY claim, Finding or not — write
it with explicit citations (document/section/page) and reasoning a reviewer could audit line by
line; a correct determination with a
vague, citation-free note still scores as a weak note (see the quality bar in the schema
field's own description).

rationale_letter is a SEPARATE, formal appeal-ready letter to the provider — only written when
determination is Finding (null otherwise). It restates the finding and its basis for an
external, non-technical reader, not a repeat of system_note's internal auditor reasoning.

Page numbers: a medical-record note can span several PDF pages, and its page_start/page_end
are not the page of any particular line in it. In a long note's text, a [p.N] marker means the
text after it (up to the next marker) is on physical page N; cite that page in system_note,
never a note's page_start/page_end range. A note whose page_start equals its page_end is all on
that page. In a multi-page note with no marker before the line, name the note without a page.

evidence_cited must reference only passages that actually appear in the retrieved rows above.
Each entry is the source_id of the one row the quote comes from, copied exactly, and the quote
copied verbatim from that row's text, character for character: don't wrap part of it in
quotation marks, fix a typo, or drop a word or code from the middle. Never invent or recall one. Code checks each quote
against that row and fills in the document, section and page from it, so a quote that isn't in
the cited row, or a source_id that wasn't retrieved, is dropped. Each quote is ONE contiguous
passage from a single row: if you need two separate passages, give two separate evidence_cited
entries rather than joining them with "..."; a stitched-together quote can't be verified. Rows
with no source_id (claim lines, code descriptions, a tool's own summary rows) aren't citable;
cite the record or policy row behind them instead.

Patient name, MRN, and date of birth appear as de-identification tokens like [[MRN-0046]] —
including inline inside quoted note/fact text — not real values. Reproduce them exactly as
given in system_note, rationale_letter, and evidence_cited quotes; a separate step restores
the real values afterward. Never remark on the token format or guess/reconstruct what it stands
for.

discharge_disposition, finding_reason, recovery_type, skilled_services,
adjusted_date_of_service, corrected_revenue_code, adjusted_units_billed,
revised_diagnosis_set, and revised_procedure_set are only meaningful for specific review types
(DRG, Readmission, SNF, SNF, SNF, SNF, DRG, and DRG respectively) — see each field's own schema
description and this review type's domain notes above to know whether to populate it; leave it
null when this review type doesn't call for it.

If this is a DRG review: you are deciding for the WHOLE claim in one pass, not one line — check
every diagnosis and procedure line given to you (POA, CC/MCC tier, whether it's still
supported), not just the one the question happens to name first. revised_diagnosis_set and
revised_procedure_set must each be the claim's COMPLETE corrected list (every code that should
remain billed, in the same shape as what you were given, position 1 = principal diagnosis) —
not a delta of only the line(s) that changed. code_decisions is what's scored: one entry per
billed code, each exactly once, plus additions, with the POA and CC/MCC tier each diagnosis
should carry, and the evidence_cited IDs behind every change. Code checks it and builds the
corrected lists from it.

Question: Audit DRG claim MR_14's full coding for this admission — this is ONE determination for the whole stay, not per code, but check every line below (not just the first) since any one of them can drive the claim-level determination.
This claim has 25 billed lines — DO NOT call get_condition_policy on every one of them, and don't run a separate medical-record search per code either; both will overflow the retrieval model's context window well before you reach a determination (verified: this happened on a 19-line claim). Teach-back is documented\nfor each session. Learning barriers: critical illness and delirium early in the course; participation improved with recovery. Interpreter not\nrequired (English).\nNorepinephrine (Levophed)\nPurpose Raises blood pressure when the body is in shock.\nDose & Route Titrated via IV infusion to maintain blood pressure.\nSide Effects Decreased blood flow to hands/feet; irregular heartbeat.\nMonitoring Continuous blood pressure and heart rate monitoring.\nTeach-Back Family verbalized understanding that the medicine keeps blood pressure safe.\nVancomycin\nPurpose Antibiotic to treat the blood infection (sepsis) and potential MRSA.\nDose & Route Individualized IV dosing based on kidney function and blood levels.\nSide Effects Kidney injury (monitored daily); rash if given too fast (Red Man Syndrome).\nMonitoring Daily labs; infuse slowly over at least 60 minutes.\nTeach-Back Family able to state purpose; instructed to report rash or skin flushing.\nPiperacillin-tazobactam (Zosyn)\nPurpose Broad-spectrum antibiotic targeting pneumonia and gram-negative bacteria.\nDose & Route 4.5 g IV every 6 hours, extended infusion over 3 hours.\nSide Effects Diarrhea; low potassium; allergic reaction (report rash immediately).\nMonitoring Renal function, electrolytes daily.\nTeach-Back Teach-back deferred - patient sedated. Education provided to son.\nPantoprazole (Protonix)\nPurpose Protects the stomach lining while on stress-ulcer prophylaxis.\nDose & Route 40 mg IV once daily, transitioning to oral when tolerating feeds.\nSide Effects Low magnesium with long-term use (monitored); headache.\nMonitoring Magnesium levels weekly; discontinue at discharge if no indication.\nTeach-Back Patient verbalized that medication protects the stomach.\nEnoxaparin (Lovenox)\nPurpose Blood thinner to prevent blood clots (DVT) in legs and lungs.\nDose & Route Prophylactic dose; adjusted if active clot is confirmed.\nSide Effects Bruising at injection site; bleeding (report blood in urine/stool).\n[p.213] Monitoring Daily CBC; watch for signs of bleeding.\nTeach-Back Son acknowledged understanding of clot-prevention purpose and verbalized when to call\nfor help (unusual bleeding).\nInsulin infusion / Sliding scale\nPurpose Controls blood sugar (glucose) which rises during critical illness.\nDose & Route IV infusion titrated to glucose 140-180 mg/dL; transitioned to SC at recovery.\nSide Effects\nLow blood sugar (hypoglycemia): sweating, confusion, shakiness.\nMonitoring Point-of-care glucose every 1-2 hours while on infusion.\nTeach-Back Patient able to describe symptoms of low blood sugar at discharge planning.\nAmiodarone\nPurpose Corrects and prevents rapid irregular heartbeat (atrial fibrillation).\nDose & Route IV load then oral maintenance; dose adjusted per response.\nSide Effects Thyroid problems, lung toxicity, liver effects (all monitored). Sensitivity to sunlight - use\nsunscreen.\nMonitoring Thyroid/liver labs monthly; chest X-ray annually; QT interval on ECG.\nTeach-Back Family verbalized that patient needs ongoing monitoring after discharge. Written materials\nprovided.\nApixaban (Eliquis) - at discharge\nPurpose Blood thinner for catheter-associated DVT (blood clot in neck vein).\nDose & Route 10 mg twice daily x 7 days, then 5 mg twice daily x at least 3 months.\nSide Effects Increased bleeding risk - avoid NSAIDs, aspirin without physician approval.\nMonitoring No routine lab monitoring required, but report unusual bleeding.\nTeach-Back Patient and son demonstrated understanding of dose schedule and verbalized to avoid\nibuprofen. result.rationale_letter: To: Medical Records / Coding Department Re: Audit determination for inpatient claim MR_14 (Admission 05/29/2026-10/10/2026) We completed a DRG audit of claim MR_14. After review of the medical record and applicable coding policy, we find the claim requires correction (Finding). Basis for finding: 1) Principal diagnosis sequencing: The admitting History & Physical and imaging document severe necrotizing gallstone pancreatitis with 40-50% pancreatic necrosis (History & Physical, p.861). The discharge summary and problem list document infected pancreatic necrosis with Klebsiella pneumoniae treated with CT-guided percutaneous drainage and video-assisted retroperitoneal debridement (Discharge / Transfer Summary, p.1085). The billed principal code K85.90 (acute pancreatitis without necrosis) is not supported by this documentation. The correct principal diagnosis is the infected necrotizing pancreatitis documented in the chart. 2) Sepsis coding and organism specificity: The chart documents vasopressor-dependent shock with lactate >2 mmol/L (Critical Care Progress Note, p.946; History & Physical, p.861) and identifies Klebsiella pneumoniae as the causative organism (Discharge / Transfer Summary, p.1085). Policy requires organism-specific sepsis coding when the organism is identified; the mapping within the policy indicates Klebsiella pneumoniae -> A41.53 and that a separate B96.x organism-only code is not required when A41.53 is used. Therefore A41.50 and B96.1 as billed are incorrect - the sepsis code should be A41.53 and B96.1 removed. R65.21 (severe sepsis with septic shock) is supported by documented vasopressor use and elevated lactate and remains an MCC where present. 3) Procedure/technique mismatch: The chart documents CT-guided percutaneous drainage and video-assisted retroperitoneal debridement (VARD) (Discharge / Transfer Summary, p.1085). The billed ICD-10-PCS 0FBG3ZZ (Excision of pancreas, percutaneous approach) denotes excision of pancreatic tissue via a percutaneous approach and is not supported by the operative description of VARD (debridement). Therefore 0FBG3ZZ should be removed; percutaneous drainage (0F9G30Z) and other line/ventilation codes remain supported. Corrections being made: - Principal diagnosis changed from K85.90 to K85.82 (other acute pancreatitis with infected necrosis) as principal. - Replace A41.50 with A41.53 (sepsis due to Klebsiella pneumoniae); remove B96.1 as redundant per policy guidance. - Retain R65.21 (severe sepsis with septic shock) given documented vasopressor requirement and lactate elevation. - Remove K85.11 and K85.90 (codes indicating uninfected or no necrosis) as not supported by imaging and operative course. - Remove procedure 0FBG3ZZ (Excision of pancreas, percutaneous approach) as unsupported by the operative documentation (VARD described). Keep procedures supported by notes (endotracheal intubation and ventilation, percutaneous drainage, PICC/lines, prolonged ventilation). Key evidence cited (examples): - History & Physical (Admitting), p.861: Imaging confirmed severe necrotizing pancreatitis with 40-50% pancreatic necrosis and cholelithiasis as the presumptive etiology. - Discharge / Transfer Summary, p.1085: infected pancreatic necrosis with Klebsiella pneumoniae treated with meropenem and a step-up approach including CT-guided percutaneous drainage on ICU day 13 followed by video-assisted retroperitoneal debridement on ICU day 16; extubation ICU day 18. - Critical Care Progress Note, p.946: vasopressors on; Lac: 5.0; P/F 73. - Procedure Note - Endotracheal Intubation, p.44: RSI with etomidate and rocuronium. Placement confirmed clinically and radiographically. - Sepsis policy (Validation Criteria): vasopressor requirement + lactate >2 and organism-specific coding rules (Klebsiella -> A41.53). If you disagree with these changes, please provide the specific clinical documentation (dated and signed provider note or lab/culture result with provider attribution) showing either (a) an explicit, dated provider statement that the principal reason for admission was sepsis (which would alter principal sequencing) or (b) documentation that the pancreatic necrosis was definitively uninfected and no organism-specific sepsis diagnosis applies. Absent that documentation, the corrections listed above will stand. Sincerely, Senior Clinical Claims Auditor

code_decisions.reason: Unrecognized/garbage code on claim with no supporting documentation in the chart; not present in problem lists or discharge diagnoses (discharge summary shows the documented diagnoses). [Discharge summary p.1085] (ev2).

Claimed principal K85.90 (acute pancreatitis without necrosis) contradicts imaging and admitting assessment documenting 40-50% pancreatic necrosis and infected necrosis (H&P p.861; Discharge summary p.1085). Remove and replace with infected necrotizing pancreatitis code.

K85.11 denotes biliary acute pancreatitis with uninfected necrosis; the record documents infected pancreatic necrosis due to Klebsiella and procedures for infected necrosis (percutaneous drainage and VARD), so the uninfected-necrosis code is not supported.

Record documents infected/necrotizing gallstone pancreatitis (imaging and problem list) and a course of drainage and debridement; K85.82 (other acute pancreatitis with infected necrosis) is the appropriate principal diagnosis and was present on admission per H&P and imaging.

No documentation of diverticulitis with perforation/abscess was found in the H&P, consults, or discharge summary; discharge problem list and hospital course document necrotizing pancreatitis and its complications instead (discharge summary p.1085).
Cholelithiasis is stated as the presumptive etiology of the gallstone pancreatitis in the admitting H&P; it is a documented comorbidity present on admission.

Septic shock physiology is supported by documented vasopressor use and elevated lactate (>2 mmol/L) with organ dysfunction (respiratory failure, AKI); policy allows coding R65.21 when vasopressor requirement and lactate support septic shock. Documentation of infected pancreatic necrosis and organism identification further supports severe sepsis/septic shock coding.

The record identifies Klebsiella pneumoniae as the infecting organism. Policy maps Klebsiella pneumoniae to A41.53 (sepsis due to Klebsiella pneumoniae); therefore recode A41.50 -> A41.53 and mark POA=Y (organism identified on admission/course).
Policy indicates that when an organism-specific sepsis code (A41.53) is assigned for Klebsiella pneumoniae, an additional B96.x organism code is not required; remove B96.1 as redundant.

Acute hypoxemic respiratory failure is documented with objective hypoxemia (low PaO2 / low P/F) and invasive mechanical ventilation (ETT), satisfying the policy validation criteria for J96.01; present on admission (intubated in ED/SICU).

Pulmonology documents moderate-severe ARDS with pancreatitis as the inciting event; ARDS is documented to have developed/required proning and later resolved prior to LTAC transfer (not present on admission).
Acute kidney injury is documented on admission with elevated creatinine and BUN and is carried through the hospital course with subsequent recovery; N17.9 is supported and present on admission.
New-onset atrial fibrillation is documented in the hospital course (cardioverted on ICU day 21/discharge summary) and therefore is a supported secondary diagnosis developing during the admission.
New-onset diabetes mellitus from pancreatic beta-cell destruction is documented in the discharge summary and problem list; retain as a secondary diagnosis (not POA).
Exocrine pancreatic insufficiency is documented at discharge, consistent with the necrotizing pancreatitis course; retain as a secondary diagnosis.
Chronic hypertension is listed in the H&P as a prior condition and is present on admission; keep as a non-CC comorbidity.
Hyperlipidemia documented in the H&P as pre-existing; keep as present on admission.
GERD documented in history; keep as present on admission.
Endotracheal intubation is documented with RSI and radiographic confirmation; keep code for ETT insertion.
Enteral feeding via nasojejunal/PEG route is documented throughout the critical phase and PEG site is recorded at discharge; keep feeding device insertion code as supported by the record.

0FBG3ZZ describes excision of pancreas via percutaneous approach; the operative note describes video-assisted retroperitoneal debridement (VARD), a debridement procedure, not a percutaneous pancreatic excision. The documentation does not support 0FBG3ZZ as billed.
CT-guided percutaneous drainage of infected pancreatic collections is explicitly described; keep percutaneous drainage of the pancreas code.
Retroperitoneal drain in place with expected output and percutaneous drainage procedures are documented; retention of peritoneal/retroperitoneal drainage code is supported by the record.
PICC line for IV antibiotics at transfer is documented in the discharge summary; insertion of an infusion device with tip in the SVC is supported.
The H&P and ICU orders document arterial-line monitoring; insertion of a monitoring device into an upper artery is supported.
Mechanical ventilation was initiated on admission and the chart documents extubation on ICU day 18 (>96 hours); the prolonged ventilation assistance code is supported.
